nameStory: The name 'crane's-bill' comes from the distinctive long, pointed seed capsules that look remarkably like a crane's beak stretching skyward. When the seeds are ripe, these 'beaks' suddenly spring open and catapult the seeds away from the parent plant. The 'small-flowered' part of the name distinguishes this petite European import from its showier native cousins.
description: Small-flowered crane's-bill is a low-growing annual herb that often goes unnoticed in disturbed places like parking lot edges and vacant lots. This unassuming plant typically stays close to the ground, rarely reaching more than 8 inches tall, with a sprawling habit. Its tiny pink or white flowers are much smaller than those of our native wild geraniums, and its deeply divided leaves give it a delicate, almost ferny appearance. Originally from Europe, it has quietly made itself at home throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink or white flowers, usually less than half an inch across, with five rounded petals that often have notched tips. The flowers are so small you might need to crouch down to really appreciate them, and they feel papery-thin to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, almost lacy leaves that are soft and slightly fuzzy when you run your fingers across them. Each leaf is cut into 5-7 narrow segments that radiate from a central point like fingers on a hand.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The characteristic 'crane's bill' seed pods are slender and pointed, about an inch long, standing upright like tiny green beaks. When ripe, they split dramatically and curl back, flinging seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop.'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that hugs the ground in a loose mat, rarely standing more than 8 inches tall. Stems are slender and often reddish, with a slightly sticky feel when handled.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged opposite each other on the stem (in pairs), with long, slender leaf stalks that give the plant an open, airy appearance.

habitat: Look for small-flowered crane's-bill in disturbed soils where few other plants thrive - along sidewalk cracks, vacant lots, construction sites, and waste places. It seems to prefer spots with poor, compacted soil that gets occasional foot traffic. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy species like plantain and chickweed in urban and suburban settings throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and begin blooming by late spring, their tiny flowers easily overlooked among the fresh green growth of more prominent plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming and seed production occurs through summer, when you can often hear the soft 'pop' of exploding seed pods on warm afternoons.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue blooming and setting seed until frost, when the entire plant dies back, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the soil.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts survive winter, but seeds lie dormant in the soil, ready to germinate when warm weather returns.

funFact: The seed pods of crane's-bills are like tiny botanical cannons that can shoot their seeds up to 20 feet away, and on a quiet summer day, you can actually hear them firing with soft popping sounds as the pods explosively uncoil in the warmth!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small crane's-bills like dove's-foot crane's-bill, but small-flowered crane's-bill has more deeply divided leaves that look almost ferny. Remember: if the leaves look lacy and delicate rather than rounded and soft, you're probably looking at small-flowered crane's-bill.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums (genus Geranium) with the colorful geraniums sold at garden centers, which are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. The crane's-bills are the true wild geraniums, and they're much more subtle in their beauty.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked. Wild geranium has showy purple-pink flowers an inch across, while small-flowered crane's-bill has flowers less than half that size. Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments and a stronger smell, while this species has more thread-like leaf divisions and little odor.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
